title: Reverse Proxies vs Forward Proxies
summary: Who each proxy type hides from whom, what a reverse proxy adds beyond plain load balancing, and where NGINX, HAProxy, and Envoy each fit.

slides.markdown:
A **proxy** is any server that sits between two parties and forwards traffic on one side's behalf. Which side it protects is the whole distinction: a **forward proxy** hides the client from the server it's talking to; a **reverse proxy** hides the server (or fleet of servers) from the client.

Every load balancer you've met so far is technically a reverse proxy that also balances load — this topic separates the two ideas and covers what a reverse proxy adds beyond just picking a backend.

slides.sectionTitle: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy: who they hide
slides.markdown:
A **forward proxy** sits in front of clients and forwards their requests outward — the destination server sees the proxy's IP, not the client's. A company's outbound web proxy is the classic example: every employee's browser traffic to the internet goes through it, so external sites see one corporate proxy IP, not thousands of individual laptops.

A **reverse proxy** sits in front of servers and forwards requests inward — the client sees the proxy's address, not any individual backend server's. When you hit `api.example.com`, you're talking to a reverse proxy that decides which of many backend servers actually answers.

Same mechanism, opposite side of the conversation being hidden.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: forward proxy (hides the client) vs reverse proxy (hides the server)
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: two side-by-side panels; left panel shows several client icons all routing through one forward-proxy box before reaching the open internet, labelled "servers see one proxy IP, not each client"; right panel shows one client icon hitting a reverse-proxy box which forwards to several backend-server icons behind it, labelled "client sees one address, not any backend" >>>

In the forward-proxy panel, the proxy is on the client's side of the conversation — it's the servers on the internet that never see the real clients. In the reverse-proxy panel, the proxy is on the server's side — it's the client that never sees which specific backend answered.

The visual test: if the proxy is protecting the identity of whoever is asking, it's forward; if it's protecting the identity of whoever is answering, it's reverse.

slides.sectionTitle: What a reverse proxy adds: TLS termination, compression, caching
slides.markdown:
A reverse proxy that only picked a backend would just be a load balancer. What makes it a reverse *proxy* is the extra work it does on every request before or after forwarding it.

**TLS termination**: the proxy decrypts HTTPS from the client and can talk plain HTTP to backends on a trusted internal network, so backend servers don't each need certificates. **Compression**: it can gzip a response before sending it to the client, saving bandwidth without every backend implementing it. **Caching**: it can serve a repeated response (a product page, a static API result) straight from its own cache without touching a backend at all.

These are why production stacks almost always put NGINX, HAProxy, or Envoy in front of app servers even when there's only one backend.

slides.sectionTitle: NGINX, HAProxy, and Envoy: what each is optimized for
slides.markdown:
All three can act as a reverse proxy and load balancer, but they grew up solving different problems.

| | Optimized for | Notable strength |
|---|---|---|
| **NGINX** | Serving web content + reverse-proxying HTTP | Extremely efficient static-file serving, huge ecosystem |
| **HAProxy** | Pure L4/L7 load balancing | Very high connection throughput, mature health checking |
| **Envoy** | Service-to-service traffic in microservices/service meshes | Dynamic config via APIs (xDS), rich observability, gRPC support |

**How to decide:** NGINX for a classic web-facing reverse proxy that also serves static files, HAProxy when raw load-balancing throughput and battle-tested failover matter most, Envoy when you're building a service mesh or need traffic managed dynamically without restarts.

slides.sectionTitle: API gateway vs reverse proxy: where the line blurs
slides.markdown:
An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy with application-aware responsibilities bolted on: authentication, rate limiting per API key, request/response transformation, and routing to dozens of backend microservices by path or version.

The line blurs because a sufficiently configured NGINX or Envoy *is* effectively acting as an API gateway — the distinction is more about role than raw technology. A plain reverse proxy asks "which server handles this?"; a gateway also asks "is this caller allowed to, and how many times have they asked this minute?"

In interviews, naming a component "API gateway" is shorthand for signaling it owns cross-cutting policy, not just routing.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: conflating "load balancer" and "reverse proxy" as the same thing
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Load balancer" and "reverse proxy" are just two names for the same component.

**Why it's wrong:** they overlap heavily in practice, but they name different responsibilities. A **load balancer**'s job is choosing which backend handles a request. A **reverse proxy**'s job is standing in for the backend tier from the client's point of view — which can include load balancing, but also TLS termination, caching, and compression, none of which is about *which* server gets picked.

**Correct model:** most production reverse proxies (NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy) also load-balance, so the terms get used interchangeably — but a pure L4 load balancer that does nothing else, and a caching reverse proxy with only one backend, are both real, non-overlapping examples that show the concepts are separable.
